g.text: Deleting an agent — ask what it would break, then break only what was agreed
systems that each hold part of the fact
references the agent. Latest only: a team
that no longer uses it is not broken going
forward, and destroying it would trade real
work for a historical version nobody deploys.
sorted by name — completion order is arbitrary once the reads overlap
2 · ask, naming what is at stake
2 teams use it and will be deleted:
The account is kept, so you can publish to it again later.
The read was the only cost.
3 · remove, in an order that survives interruption
[for each referencing team, stopping at the first failure]
the team no longer answers mentions
the observer trails the validator, so a plain refetch can resurrect them
the rows are gone, and stay gone
Why this order, and not the reverse.
Unpublishing needs the credential the publication was made with,
and that credential is reached *through* the team record. Delete the team first and a failed unpublish
strands a live handle answering for a team that no longer exists, with the means to stop it destroyed
alongside it. Unpublish first and the worst interruption leaves a team that is merely unpublished —
visible, intact, and republishable. The agent goes last for the same reason: an interruption then leaves
teams pointing at an agent that still exists, rather than the dangling references this whole flow exists
PDS — the handle and its config record
